```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(targets)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(gt)

## Suppresses terra's own text progress bar ("|---------|.../===...") for
## slow calls on this report's large, disk-backed rasters (e.g.
## raster_mean_series()'s terra::global() on monthly_gpp_rast, fig-gpp-
## spliced-record below) -- raw console output, not an R condition, so the
## YAML's own execute: warning/message: false above never touched it (found
## live 2026-09, appearing as stray text between two figures in the
## rendered report).
terra::terraOptions(progress = 0)

## Handle both pipeline rendering (from project root) and standalone rendering
## (from inside quarto_reports/), same convention as raw_data_update.qmd.
store_path <- if (dir.exists("_targets")) "_targets" else "../_targets"
r_path     <- if (dir.exists("_targets")) "r" else "../r"

## raster_mean_series() (r/b_raster_mean_series.R) -- collapses a SpatRaster
## to a tidy one-row-per-layer mean series, nationally or at points, used
## throughout this report. mask_gpp_offshore()/clamp_gpp_sentinel_codes()
## (r/b_mask_gpp_offshore.R, r/b_clamp_gpp_sentinel_codes.R) -- the two real
## masking steps, reused directly (not reimplemented) for
## fig-gpp-masking-coastal-detail's own before/after panels. All sourced
## directly (not tar_load()'d, since they're plain functions, not targets)
## so this report and the pipeline itself share one implementation instead
## of the qmd keeping its own local copy.
##
## Every OTHER GPP function this report used to source live
## (load_and_clamp_gpp_composites(), finish_gpp_period_raster(),
## apply_gpp_pixel_ratio_correction(), convert_gpp_to_daily_rate(),
## aggregate_gpp_to_periods()) has since been dropped (2026-09) -- the
## "NASA pixel-scale corrections and splice" figure group (fig-splice-
## continuity) used to recompute national means live from
## native-resolution composite/monthly rasters via these functions
## (~25GB/1196 layers and ~5.8GB/319 layers respectively, confirmed the
## two most expensive lines in this report); it now reuses already-
## cheap, already-tar_load()'d gpp_monthly_df/gpp_corrected_paddock_mean
## instead (that chunk's own header explains why) -- see "NASA
## pixel-scale corrections and splice" below for the full reasoning that
## substitution relies on. A separate national-mean-vs-paddock-mean
## report figure, fig-gpp-all-sources, was merged into fig-splice-
## continuity entirely (2026-09) once both were confirmed to be
## checking the same raw-vs-corrected question, just at a different
## grain/zoom -- see fig-splice-continuity's own header.
source(file.path(r_path, "b_raster_mean_series.R"))
source(file.path(r_path, "b_mask_gpp_offshore.R"))
source(file.path(r_path, "b_clamp_gpp_sentinel_codes.R"))

## Every src-targets-step-* chunk below is a pasted-in copy of _targets.R's
## own GPP section, one step at a time -- kept in sync manually rather than
## via knitr::read_chunk()/<<name>> referencing. That was tried first
## (2026-09, alongside the #| file: "../r/..." fix every function-reference
## chunk below DOES use successfully): each step was bracketed with its own
## "# @knitr gpp-step-<roman numeral>" marker in _targets.R, and each chunk
## here referenced it via <<gpp-step-x>>, reading _targets.R fresh every
## render with no possible drift -- and it worked for a real `quarto render`
## of this file directly. But it broke this project's actual pipeline:
## tarchetypes::tar_quarto() (the gpp_processing_html target, _targets.R)
## statically scans a qmd for tar_load()/tar_read() dependencies via
## knitr's own tangle mode, which needs to specially detect and evaluate any
## read_chunk() call in isolation before the rest of the document runs --
## confirmed live its detector uses a naive, non-nesting-aware paren-match
## to find that call's own closing bracket, so ANY argument containing a
## nested "(" (even a trivial `if (TRUE) "a" else "b"`) truncates mid-
## expression and throws "unexpected end of input" -- a hard limitation, not
## a bug in this document, and not fixable by varying the expression's own
## complexity or length (both tested live). A literal path can't cover both
## this document's genuine dual-mode rendering conventions (pipeline vs
## standalone, store_path/r_path above), so read_chunk() was reverted here
## in favour of periodically re-pasting each step's own current code by hand
## -- the same one-off resync process already used once this same session,
## now the ongoing maintenance cost instead of a permanent fix. The "# @knitr
## gpp-step-*" markers stay in _targets.R itself (harmless comments) so that
## resync can still be done precisely rather than by hand-matching text.
##
## composite_gpp_months_of matches _targets.R's own plan-time helper of the
## same name -- every NASA-side pixel-ratio call below (composite grain,
## date-named layers) needs it in place of build_gpp_pixel_ratio_raster()'s/
## apply_gpp_pixel_ratio_correction()'s own "<month>_<year>" default.
composite_gpp_months_of <- function(x) lubridate::month(as.Date(x))

tar_load(
  c(
    gpp_raster_coarse, monthly_gpp_rast, monthly_gpp_rast_coarse,
    composite_gpp_rast_modis, composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf, composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf_frozen, composite_gpp_rast_viirs_nongf,
    composite_gpp_rast_modis_corrected, composite_gpp_rast_viirs_nongf_corrected,
    pml_gpp_rast, pml_gpp_rast_corrected,
    gpp_pml_bias_check, gpp_pml_pixel_ratio_rast,
    gpp_gf_bias_check, gpp_gf_pixel_ratio_rast,
    gpp_modis_bias_check, gpp_modis_pixel_ratio_rast,
    gpp_modis_national_mean, gpp_viirs_gf_national_mean, gpp_viirs_nongf_national_mean,
    gpp_pml_paddock_mean, gpp_modis_paddock_mean, gpp_viirs_gf_paddock_mean,
    gpp_viirs_nongf_paddock_mean, gpp_corrected_paddock_mean,
    gpp_viirs_frozen_blocks, gpp_viirs_recent_blocks, gpp_files_viirs_recent_block,
    gpp_files_viirs_frozen_block, aus_shp,
    gpp_focal_raster, paddocks_sf_with_soil_type
  ),
  store = store_path
)

## Years covered by each of the two most recent (non-frozen) GPP blocks --
## used below to report the frozen/recent boundary in prose without
## hard-coding it.
gpp_recent_years <- sort(unlist(gpp_viirs_recent_blocks))
gpp_last_frozen_year <- max(unlist(gpp_viirs_frozen_blocks))

## The actual latest calendar year with a COMPLETE set of real gap-filled
## VIIRS composites -- distinct from gpp_last_frozen_year (above), which is
## the pipeline's own permanently-cached boundary, not a statement about how
## much gap-filled data NASA has actually published. gpp_last_frozen_year
## always trails this by design (the "recent" window keeps last year's block
## re-checked for a full extra year before promoting it to frozen, see i./
## "Why targets" below) -- so a year can be fully gap-filled in reality while
## still sitting in the "recent" bucket, exactly the gap this checks for.
## Computed live from the actual downloaded composite files (not hard-typed)
## so this can't quietly drift out of date the way a fixed year would.
gf_recent_dates <- {
  gf_files <- gpp_files_viirs_recent_block[grepl("Gpp_500m.*\\.tif$", gpp_files_viirs_recent_block)]
  as.Date(sub(".*doy([0-9]{4})([0-9]{3}).*", "\\1-\\2", gf_files), format = "%Y-%j")
}
gf_complete_recent_years <- Filter(function(y) {
  expected <- as.Date(paste(y, seq(1, 361, by = 8), sep = "-"), format = "%Y-%j")
  all(expected %in% gf_recent_dates)
}, gpp_recent_years)
gpp_gf_latest_complete_year <- max(c(gpp_last_frozen_year, gf_complete_recent_years))

## PML's own pre-2000 layers -- the portion actually spliced into the record
## (see apply_gpp_pixel_ratio_correction()). Used below for the national-
## vs-paddock GPP-level comparison.
pml_pre2000_layers <- names(pml_gpp_rast)[as.integer(sub(".*_", "", names(pml_gpp_rast))) < 2000]
pml_pre2000_rast    <- pml_gpp_rast[[pml_pre2000_layers]]
pml_pre2000_months  <- as.integer(sub("_.*", "", names(pml_pre2000_rast)))

pml_paddock_monthly_mean <- gpp_pml_paddock_mean |>
  dplyr::filter(lubridate::year(date) < 2000) |>
  dplyr::mutate(month = lubridate::month(date)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(month) |>
  dplyr::summarise(value = mean(value), .groups = "drop")

## National-mean counterpart to pml_paddock_monthly_mean, same pre-2000
## years -- referenced alongside it to illustrate the national/paddock gap
## inline rather than as hand-transcribed numbers.
pml_national_monthly_mean <- tibble::tibble(
  month = pml_pre2000_months,
  value = terra::global(pml_pre2000_rast, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
) |>
  dplyr::group_by(month) |>
  dplyr::summarise(value = mean(value), .groups = "drop")

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom")
)

## Computed once here and reused everywhere below -- gpp_raster_coarse (not
## monthly_gpp_rast) specifically: same full 1982-present monthly record,
## already resampled onto PML's coarse 0.1 degree grid, so terra::global()'s
## spatial mean is cheap here instead of running it over 300+ layers at
## GPP's native 500m resolution.
gpp_monthly_df <- raster_mean_series(gpp_raster_coarse) |>
  dplyr::mutate(recent_block = lubridate::year(date) %in% gpp_recent_years)
gpp_latest_month <- format(max(gpp_monthly_df$date), "%B %Y")
```

## Overview

**Gross Primary Productivity (GPP)** is the rate at which plants fix atmospheric carbon via photosynthesis, in grams of carbon per square metre per day (gC/m²/day).

GPP is a standard satellite-derived proxy for how fast vegetation has potential to grow -- crop yields, or pasture growth. My purpose is to use GPP as a proxy for crop yields, as patterns in crop yields are likely to be indicative of food availability for house mice in cropping regions. **I therefore use GPP as a predictor variable in statistical forecast models which aim to predict mouse population outbreaks at seasonal time steps**. I have mouse population survey data dating back to the late 1970's, so I need a continuous GPP measure from this period to the present.

No single satellite product provides a long, continuous, standardised GPP record on its own -- the two modern standards (MODIS, VIIRS) don't reach back before 2000, and only a differently-modelled historical product (PML-V2) covers the gap (as far as I am aware). So here, GPP **is spliced from four raw products into one continuous monthly record from 1982 to the present.**.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gpp-splice-timeline
#| fig-cap: "How the continuous 1982-present GPP record is built: which raw product supplies it at each point in time (top), and the periods used to bias-correct all three splices between them (bottom)."
#| fig-asp: 0.32

## Real archive/coverage boundaries, computed live from data already loaded
## above -- not hard-typed -- so this figure can't quietly drift out of sync
## with the record it's describing.
pml_archive_end_year <- max(as.integer(sub(".*_", "", names(pml_gpp_rast))))  # PML-V2's own TPDC archive end (2020)
record_end_year       <- lubridate::year(max(gpp_monthly_df$date))            # latest month in the actual spliced record

splice_segments <- tibble::tribble(
  ~source,                                             ~start_year,                    ~end_year,
  "PML-V2 (ratio-corrected)",                          1982,                           1999,
  "MODIS (ratio-corrected)",                           2000,                           2011,
  "VIIRS GF",                                          2012,                           gpp_gf_latest_complete_year,
  "VIIRS NGF (ratio-corrected fallback)",              gpp_gf_latest_complete_year + 1, record_end_year
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(source = factor(source, levels = source))

## All three splices now get a computed pixel-scale ratio correction (2026-08
## -- MODIS into VIIRS is no longer left uncorrected, see "How well do the
## four GPP products agree?" below) -- each correction's own window is the
## real composite-date overlap the two NASA sources share (intersect() inside
## build_gpp_pixel_ratio_raster(), not a separately-tracked "correction
## years" list -- that concept (r_not_in_use/b_find_gf_nongf_correction_years.R)
## was retired once every correction moved to composite grain and could just
## intersect() its own two inputs directly).
## Each correction gets its own row (own y, own line) rather than all three
## sharing one line at y = 1 -- the three windows now overlap in
## time (e.g. PML-V2 vs MOD17/VNP17's 2000-2020 fully contains MOD17 vs VNP17
## GF's own window), so a shared line just drew as one solid overlapping bar
## with only the staggered labels hinting there were three windows at all
## (2026-09, found via user review). row (1 = top) sets each correction's own
## y via row_y below -- kept in the same earliest-start-first order as the
## tribble itself, so reading top to bottom roughly tracks reading left to
## right along the x-axis too.
## label_x/hjust for the VIIRS GF-vs-NGF one is still right-anchored on its
## own line's end (not centred) -- that window sits right at the plot's own
## right edge, so a centred label would run straight off the panel; the other
## two rows now have a whole row to themselves, so centred is fine for them.
## MOD17 vs VNP17 uses the FROZEN-only GF stack -- that's the real reference
## that correction is actually fitted from (2026-08, a caching fix -- see "iv.
## Compute NASA pixel-scale corrections" below), so showing the full stack's
## own overlap here would overstate its window. GF vs NGF still uses the full
## (frozen+recent) stack -- composite_gpp_rast_viirs_nongf only covers the
## recent ~2 years by construction, so it has zero overlap with frozen-only
## GF (confirmed live 2026-08 -- see the same section for why).
modis_viirs_overlap_years <- lubridate::year(range(as.Date(intersect(names(composite_gpp_rast_modis), names(composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf_frozen)))))
gf_nongf_overlap_years    <- lubridate::year(range(as.Date(intersect(names(composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf), names(composite_gpp_rast_viirs_nongf)))))

row_y <- c(1.4, 1.0, 0.6)  # top to bottom; evenly spaced so their mean (1.0) doubles as the axis tick position below

correction_segments <- tibble::tribble(
  ~correction,                     ~start_year,                       ~end_year,                          ~hjust,
  "PML-V2 vs MOD17/VNP17",         2000,                               pml_archive_end_year,               0.5,
  "MOD17 vs VNP17 GF",             modis_viirs_overlap_years[1],       modis_viirs_overlap_years[2] + 1,   0.5,
  "VIIRS GF vs NGF",               gf_nongf_overlap_years[1],          gf_nongf_overlap_years[2] + 1,      1
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    row_y   = row_y,
    label_x = ifelse(hjust == 1, end_year, (start_year + end_year) / 2)
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = splice_segments, aes(xmin = start_year, xmax = end_year + 1, ymin = 1.7, ymax = 2.5, fill = source)) +
  geom_segment(data = correction_segments, aes(x = start_year, xend = end_year, y = row_y, yend = row_y), colour = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = correction_segments, aes(x = label_x, y = row_y + 0.12, label = correction, hjust = hjust), vjust = 0, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1982, record_end_year, by = 4), expand = expansion(mult = 0.01)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(mean(row_y), 2.1), labels = c("Bias correction\ncomputed from", "Record spliced\nfrom"), limits = c(0.4, 2.7)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

This workflow derives two GPP products:

- **Coarse (\~11km cell resolution), monthly (average) GPP from 1982-present**: GPP resampled onto the coarsest spatial and temporal resolution source -- PML-V2's (\~11 km cells; monthly time steps). Monthly is sufficient for my own purposes too as the mouse forecast models run with seasonal time steps. The coarse spatial scale is also likely reasonable given mouse plagues occur over broad areas, and so it is important to capture landscape-scale resources rather than focus on finer-scale patterns near some paddocks.
- **Fine (3×3-cell focal-window average at native 500m resolution) monthly (average, but trimmed to end of season months) GPP from 2000-present**: spliced MODIS/VIIRS products only. Restricting to season-end months keeps the (relatively expensive, native-resolution) focal-smoothing step to a quarter of the layers it would otherwise process, since no downstream consumer ever reads a value from any other month. This is primarily for use as a rapid assessment method covariate which were introduced from 2012 onwards (e.g., to account for vegetation obscuring active burrow searches; and perhaps affecting chew cards).

Every processing step is automated through R code and integrated into an **R analysis pipeline to allow seasonal mouse plague forecasting in near real time**, built using the R package [`targets`](https://books.ropensci.org/targets/) -- it tracks which functions and variables each step depends on, and only recomputes a step if something it depends on has changed since the last run, rather than rebuilding everything from scratch every time, which matters here since GPP's own downloads/raster builds can run for hours. Every step described here is one stage of that pipeline -- see below for the exact code, the full source of every function it calls, and (in the download step specifically) how that incremental behaviour governs when a new download actually happens.

![Schematic of the 'targets' R pipeline used to forecast mouse plagues -- GPP is one input variable, alongside mouse survey data (live-trapping, rapid assessment, farmer observations), predicting at seasonal time-steps.](images/pipeline_schematic.png){#fig-pipeline-schematic}

This report covers how each source is processed, including how all three splices between them are corrected for bias in different measurements (PML-V2, historical MODIS, and real-time / unprocessed VIIRS). GPP is further summarised for modelling (e.g., anomalies) but this is not covered in this report.

### Broad processing steps

The pipeline is organised into three independent parts: **A) NASA** (MODIS/VIIRS, end to end -- download, correct, splice, mask, aggregate -- with no dependency on PML at all), **B) PML** (download and crop only), and **C) Combine** (bias-check, correct and splice PML's own pre-2000 record in underneath NASA's finished one). This produces two separate finished GPP products, at two different points in this same sequence: the coarse, PML-spliced product (1982-present, step 8 below) that C) finishes, and a fine-scale product (2000-present, step 9 below) that branches directly off A)'s own finished record instead -- never touching PML at any point.

1. **A) NASA.** Download MODIS/VIIRS's own native 8-day composites.
2. Load composites, clamp sensor sentinel/fill codes, convert to a common mean daily rate (gC/m²/day) -- still at native \~500m resolution, one layer per composite date, not yet masked to the coastline or aggregated to a period.
3. Cross-check MOD17 against VNP17, and non-gap-filled VIIRS against gap-filled, at this same composite grain.
4. Compute a pixel-scale, per-calendar-month ratio correction for both (MOD17 towards VNP17; non-gap-filled VIIRS towards gap-filled), and apply it.
5. Splice every corrected NASA source into one continuous composite-grain stack, most-robust-source-first (gap-filled VIIRS, then corrected non-gap-filled VIIRS, then corrected MOD17).
6. Mask off-shore cells and aggregate to a common monthly grain -- deferred to this last step, once, rather than four times per raw source -- producing NASA's own finished, self-contained monthly record (`monthly_gpp_rast`).
7. **B) PML.** Download PML-V2's own native monthly composites, crop and mask to the study area (no aggregation needed -- PML-V2 is already monthly).
8. **C) Combine.** Resample NASA's finished monthly record onto PML-V2's own coarser 0.1° grid, bias-check PML against it over their real 2000-2020 overlap, compute a pixel-scale ratio correction for PML and apply it, then splice corrected PML in underneath NASA's own record (PML only ever supplies 1982-1999, where NASA has nothing) -- **finalising the coarse GPP product** (`gpp_raster_coarse`, 1982-present, one continuous grid throughout).
9. **Fine GPP** (branches from step 6, not from the combined record above): crop NASA's own finished monthly record to whichever states' paddocks need it, then focal-smooth and season-end-trim it (see the fine-scale bullet above for why) -- **finalising the fine-scale GPP product** (`gpp_focal_raster`, 2000-present, NASA-only, never resampled onto a coarser grid or spliced with PML).

## GPP Sources {#sec-gpp-sources}

### MODIS / VIIRS (2000+)

- Recent GPP values are derived from NASA using MOD17 (MODIS/Terra; due to shut down from late 2026) and its designated successor VNP17 (VIIRS). The pipeline replaces MOD17 with VNP17 in 2012, though MOD17 files downloaded over a frozen window from 2000 to `r format(max(as.Date(names(composite_gpp_rast_modis))), "%B %Y")` -- maximising overlap for accurate bias evaluation. I have not extended it further, even as new composites continue to be published, for computational efficiency.

- Both products are 8-day composites at 500 m resolution.

- Each of these products is downloaded via NASA's AppEEARS service (Application for Extracting and Exploring Analysis Ready Samples -- a free API/web tool for requesting an area/time subset of a NASA data product).

- Both calculate GPP using the light-use efficiency (LUE) approach -- *GPP = APAR × ε*

  - APAR (absorbed photosynthetically active radiation) is calculated from incoming solar radiation (from reanalysis/meteorological data) and FPAR (fraction of PAR absorbed by vegetation), which MODIS/VIIRS derives from its own remote-sensing land cover and vegetation index products (FPAR/LAI, MOD15).
  - ε (light-use efficiency) starts from a biome-specific maximum efficiency (ε_max, looked up from a biome classification map) and is then downregulated by environmental stress scalars for temperature and vapor pressure deficit (VPD), sourced from meteorological reanalysis data.

So here GPP = satellite-derived vegetation greenness × modelled radiation × biome-specific efficiency, reduced by temperature/moisture stress. The difference between MODIS and VIIRS lies in their sensor characteristics and provenance of input data (FPAR/LAI and land cover products) -- VIIRS has different spectral bands and spatial resolution handling.

![MODIS/VIIRS's light-use-efficiency (LUE) approach: satellite FPAR/LAI and land cover, combined with meteorological data, give absorbed radiation (APAR) and a stress-adjusted efficiency term (ε); GPP = APAR × ε.](images/modis_viirs_lue_pipeline.png){#fig-modis-viirs-lue-pipeline}

There are two VIIRS products used:

- **VIIRS gap-filled** (VNP17A2GF.002): 2012-`r gpp_gf_latest_complete_year` (currently). Applies quality-control screening to every 8-day LAI/FPAR input pixel first (the vegetation-greenness input the light-use-efficiency algorithm needs). Any pixel that fails that quality-control check gets discarded and replaced via linear temporal interpolation (using neighbouring good-quality composites) before GPP is even computed from it. A cloud-contaminated or otherwise low-confidence LAI/FPAR pixel still produces a GPP number — it isn't blank, it's just less trustworthy.

- **VIIRS non-gap-filled** (VNP17A2.002): `r min(gpp_recent_years)`-present. Is a near-real-time product, but uses the raw LAI/FPAR product with missing values. Cloud contamination doesn't corrupt vegetation-index retrievals randomly; it tends to systematically bias them in a consistent direction (and its frequency varies strongly by season and region).

### PML-V2 (1982-1999)

- PML-V2 (Penman-Monteith-Leuning, version 2) is a different GPP model driven by older AVHRR (Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer) satellite inputs (as MODIS/VIIRS didn't exist yet), developed from China's National Tibetan Plateau/Third Pole Environment Data Centre:

  Xu, Z., Zhang, Y., Kong, D., Ma, N., & Zhang, X. (2026). Extended global terrestrial evapotranspiration and gross primary production dataset from 1982 to near present. Earth System Science Data, 18(7), 5663-5695. <https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-5663-2026>.

- PML-V2 is available as a monthly product at a 0.1 degree (\~100 km^2^) resolution.

- PML-V2 takes a more mechanistic, coupled approach to estimating GPP rather than a simple LUE lookup model. It jointly simulates GPP and evapotranspiration within a single framework, because photosynthesis and transpiration are physically linked through stomatal conductance:

  - It uses a two-leaf (sunlit/shaded) canopy scheme to separately model photosynthesis for sunlit and shaded leaves, using remote-sensing FPAR/LAI as structural inputs.
  - Stomatal conductance is estimated and used both to constrain carbon uptake (GPP) and water loss (transpiration) simultaneously, coupling them through a shared biophysical model rather than independent statistical relationships.
  - Meteorological drivers (radiation, temperature, VPD, humidity) come from reanalysis data, similar to MODIS/VIIRS.

![PML-V2's coupled photosynthesis-transpiration model: canopy structure and meteorological drivers feed a two-leaf canopy scheme and stomatal conductance model that jointly constrain GPP and evapotranspiration -- cross-validated against each other, unlike MODIS/VIIRS's independent LUE approach.](images/pmlv2_coupled_pipeline.png){#fig-pmlv2-coupled-pipeline}

This makes PML-V2 more physically constrained than the simpler LUE models, since GPP and ET have to remain mutually consistent (calibrated/validated jointly against flux tower and water balance data), often improving accuracy in water-limited or heterogeneous canopy conditions.

### Key differences between MODIS/VIIRS and PML-V2

MODIS/VIIRS runs a single linear chain ending in one output (GPP), while PML-V2 branches at the stomatal conductance step into two outputs (GPP and ET) that constrain each other — that mutual consistency check is what gives PML-V2 its extra physical grounding, especially where water stress matters.

| Aspect | MOD17/VNP17 | PML-V2 |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| *Core theory* | Light-use efficiency (LUE) | Coupled photosynthesis–transpiration (Penman-Monteith-Leuning) |
| *Canopy treatment* | Big-leaf | Two-leaf (sunlit/shaded) |
| *Efficiency term* | Biome-lookup ε_max with stress scalars | Derived from stomatal conductance |
| *Spatial resolution* | 0.5 km | \~11 km |
| *Temporal resolution (native)* | 8-day composite (raw overpasses algorithmically combined per period) | Monthly total (a continuous model's own output, summed -- not a composite of raw observations) |
| *Date range available (from source)* | MOD17A2HGF.061 2000-present (Terra retiring 2026/27, per NASA); VNP17A2GF.002 2012-present (its successor). Non-gap-filled siblings: rolling window only, no archive | 1982-2020 -- TPDC's own fixed, completed archive (the source paper's "near present" claim isn't reflected in what's actually downloadable) |
| *Date range downloaded by this pipeline* | 2000-present\* (full archive -- only its pre-2012 portion is actually spliced in, see below) | 1982-2020 (full archive -- only its pre-2000 portion is actually spliced in) |
| *Date range spliced into the final record* | 2000-2011 | 1982-1999 |
| *Native output units* | kg C/m²/8-day (accumulated over each composite period) | gC/m²/month (accumulated over each month) |
| *Delivery* | NASA AppEEARS (on-demand, region-of-interest subset request) | TPDC FTP (bulk global NetCDF download, cropped locally) |

: Key differences between MODIS/VIIRS's light-use-efficiency approach and PML-V2's coupled photosynthesis-transpiration model -- including the resolution and unit mismatches this pipeline has to reconcile before the two can be spliced together.

\* MOD17's own "2000-present" here is looser than VIIRS's: unlike VIIRS gap-filled, which genuinely re-checks for new composites on an open-ended `todays_date` window, MODIS is downloaded up to a FROZEN end date (`gpp_modis_end_date`, currently 2026-08-21) that's only updated manually -- chasing every new day would cost a full multi-GB re-request for no real gain, since MOD17A2HGF's own gap-filled processing lags well behind real-time regardless of what end date is requested (Methods, `#### MODIS`).

## Methods {#sec-gpp-pipeline}

This section walks through \_targets.R's GPP section ("2) Gross Primary Productivity (GPP)") end to end below -- each subsection shows that step's own exact `_targets.R` code alongside the full source of every function it calls for reference only (`eval: false`). The pipeline is organised into three independent parts (see "Broad processing steps" above): **A) NASA** (steps `i.` through `vi.`, MODIS/VIIRS end to end -- download, correct, splice, mask, aggregate -- producing `monthly_gpp_rast`, NASA's own finished record with no dependency on PML at all); **B) PML** (steps `vii.`-`viii.`, download and crop only); **C) Combine** (step `ix.`, bias-check/correct/splice PML's pre-2000 record in underneath NASA's, producing the final `gpp_raster_coarse`). `x.` reports on the finished record (national/paddock mean diagnostics, this report's own figures); `xi.` builds a second, fine-scale product from NASA's own monthly record (`vi.`), not the combined `gpp_raster_coarse` -- for a different purpose (the rapid assessment detection covariate); `xii.` builds the rolling-average/anomaly/climatology covariates actually fed to the forecast model (not covered in this report -- see `covariate_summary.qmd`'s own "GPP" section instead, as noted above).

## A) NASA {#sec-gpp-nasa}

### i. Download NASA products (MODIS, VIIRS)

Three raw sources feed this step, each via a different download mechanism -- PML-V2's own download is a separate, later step (`vii.`, part B) below), since it has no bearing on NASA's own finished record:

| Product | Service | Date range downloaded | Function |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| **MODIS** | NASA AppEEARS | 2000-01-01 to a frozen end date (`gpp_modis_end_date`, currently 2026-08-21) -- not open-ended, though only its pre-2012 portion is actually spliced in (v. below) | `download_gpp()` |
| **VIIRS gap-filled** | NASA AppEEARS | 2012-present, one request per calendar year, each into its own permanent folder | `download_gpp_block()` |
| **VIIRS non-gap-filled** | NASA AppEEARS | current + previous year only, per request; checked (not re-downloaded) each run for new composites -- retained files build a growing bias-correction pool over time. | `download_gpp()` |

: How each of the three NASA-sourced raw products are downloaded within the 'targets' R pipeline.

#### MODIS

Downloads MOD17A2HGF.061 from 2000-01-01 to a FROZEN end date (`gpp_modis_end_date`, currently 2026-08-21), not open-ended via `todays_date` the way VIIRS gap-filled does below. MODIS is only ever used for the pre-2012 portion of the merged record (v. below, VIIRS supplies 2012+) and the MOD17-vs-VNP17 bias check/correction (iii./iv.), both already well served once the archive reaches a recent date -- chasing every new day buys nothing further for either use, while AppEEARS' own request handling collapses even a tiny few-date top-up into a full re-delivery of this whole multi-GB archive (\~10h/\~17GB just to add a few months of new composites; see `download_gpp()`'s own `gpp_group_contiguous_dates()` header). A fixed end date keeps this target stable instead of re-triggering that same costly re-request on every later `tar_make()` call (`recheck_after_days` can still occasionally retrigger it for a handful of permanently-missing historic dates, accepted as rare) -- and since MOD17A2HGF's own gap-filled processing lags well behind real-time regardless of what end date is requested, freezing it costs nothing further, even for the most recent data.

Even though only its pre-2012 portion ever ends up in the merged record (v. below -- VIIRS is used automatically for 2012+, so no separate trim step is needed), two reasons still justify downloading the rest of the archive: it gives [iii. Cross-product bias-check diagnostics](#sec-gpp-bias-check) a real 2012+ overlap to compare MOD17 against VNP17 directly (the same comparison PML-V2's own check later uses, `gpp_modis_bias_check`) and feeds a genuine pixel-scale correction for the MODIS/VIIRS splice (iv. below), not just this diagnostic; and it captures as much of the archive as possible before MOD17A2HGF.061's own coming retirement (NASA's guidance -- an Earthdata/NSIDC alert, May 2025 -- has Terra/Aqua beginning retirement in late 2026/early 2027). This mirrors PML-V2's own already-established pattern of downloading a full archive and letting the splice's own robustness ordering decide what's actually used (v. below).

#### VIIRS gap-filled

Uses the same `download_gpp()` function as MODIS, since both are AppEEARS-sourced with an identical layer/scale/cadence spec -- split into yearly blocks first (`build_year_blocks()`) via a thin wrapper, `download_gpp_block()`, so each calendar year gets its own permanently-isolated download folder rather than one ever-growing multi-decade request.

For computational efficiency, both VIIRS download targets (`gpp_files_viirs_frozen_block`, `gpp_files_viirs_recent_block`) are built on `targets`' own dynamic branching to do this -- `pattern = map(gpp_viirs_frozen_blocks)`/`map(gpp_viirs_recent_blocks)` turns each year-block into its own independent "branch," built and cached entirely on its own. That's what actually gives each calendar year genuine per-year isolation, not just a per-year folder on disk -- re-downloading or invalidating one year's branch never touches any other year's already-cached one.

Its raw-download targets reference the `todays_date` global directly or indirectly (via `gpp_viirs_blocks`, below), so the first `tar_make()` call on a new calendar day re-checks AppEEARS for anything newly published. Even then, re-executing a target isn't the same as a new file transferring: `download_gpp_block()` does its own internal check first (composite dates already on disk vs. expected) and only contacts AppEEARS if there's a genuine gap.

Two blocks stay in this "recent" bucket rather than one, as a safety margin: gap-filled composites can still be published late for last year even after the calendar rolls over, so freezing that block immediately would risk missing late-arriving data. A block only moves from "recent" to permanently frozen once it's had a full extra year to receive any such late publications -- so a year can already be completely gap-filled in reality while still sitting in the "recent" bucket, kept there out of caution rather than genuine incompleteness.

#### VIIRS non-gap-filled

Uses `download_gpp()` directly (not the yearly-block wrapper), requesting only the current + previous year, and shares the same `todays_date`-driven re-check behaviour as VIIRS gap-filled above. That 2-year window does two distinct jobs, not one:

- **Real-time fallback.** Gap-filled composites lag real-time by several months, so right after a new calendar year starts, gap-filled can still be missing composites from the tail end of last year -- reaching back to the start of the previous year keeps the fallback substitution covered across that boundary, not just within the current year.
- **Feeding the bias-correction pool.** A given year's non-gap-filled composites only ever get downloaded once, while that year still sits in this 2-year window -- once the window rolls forward, that year is never requested again (`download_gpp()` never deletes what's already on disk, but it also never re-fetches it), so this is the one chance to capture that year's record at all. The bias-correction pool itself isn't limited to these 2 years, though: `build_gpp_pixel_ratio_raster()` (iv. below) intersects the full accumulated gap-filled and non-gap-filled composite-grain records directly, over *every* composite date both sides happen to share, with no separate "which years qualify" pre-filter needed -- so the correction grows automatically, one more composite date at a time, every run the pipeline keeps this narrow download window capturing new data.

Keeping the record current, across all three AppEEARS-sourced products, is just a matter of running `tar_make()` periodically -- the incremental logic above handles the rest.

Before any of this can run standalone, you'll need a few accounts and packages of your own.

- For MODIS/VIIRS via AppEEARS: a free [NASA Earthdata Login](https://urs.earthdata.nasa.gov/) account, plus the `appeears` R package itself (not on CRAN -- `remotes::install_github("bluegreen-labs/appeears")`).
- For PML-V2's FTP archive: a TPDC account.
- Both download functions also need `keyring`, since they read credentials from the OS keychain rather than ever hard-coding them (see each function's own header for the one-off interactive setup call).

#### Code

```{r}
#| label: src-targets-step-i
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "_targets.R -- i. Download NASA products (MODIS, VIIRS)"

  # i. Download NASA products (MODIS, VIIRS) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  # Download MODIS (2000-01-01 to gpp_modis_end_date, gap-filled) -- FROZEN, not open-ended like VIIRS (below): MODIS is only ever used for the pre-2012 portion of the merged record (v. below, VIIRS supplies 2012+) and the MOD17-vs-VNP17 bias check/correction (iii./iv.), both already well served once the archive reaches a recent date -- chasing every new day via todays_date buys nothing further for either use, while AppEEARS' own request handling collapses even a tiny few-date top-up into a full re-delivery of this whole multi-GB archive (a single such top-up costs ~10h and ~17GB just to add a few months of new composites; see gpp_group_contiguous_dates()'s header, r/b_download_gpp.R). A fixed gpp_modis_end_date keeps this target stable once complete instead of re-triggering that same costly full re-request on every later tar_make(). recheck_after_days is raised from the function's own 7-day default to 36500 for the same reason: even the "handful of permanently-missing historic composite dates" case the 7-day default was sized for still recurs often enough in practice to periodically re-trigger this, this pipeline's single most expensive target (~6h just to reload/clamp the archive after a successful transfer, on top of the AppEEARS request itself) -- MODIS is capped/frozen precisely because the current archive already more than covers its only two uses above, so there is no genuine benefit to ever automatically retrying that permanent gap again; a real reason to re-request MODIS (e.g. deliberately extending gpp_modis_end_date) should be a manual, deliberate action, not something recheck_after_days' own cooldown ever does on its own.
  tar_file(gpp_files_modis, download_gpp(
    roi                 = covariate_download_region,
    out_dir             = "raw_data/predictor_variables/gpp/modis",
    earthdata_user      = "mwr25",
    product             = "MOD17A2HGF.061",
    start_date          = "2000-01-01",
    end_date            = gpp_modis_end_date,
    job_name            = paste0("gpp_modis_", format(Sys.Date(), "%Y%m%d")),
    time_out            = 28800,
    recheck_after_days  = 36500)),

  # MODIS's own 5-year calendar blocks -- so composite_gpp_rast_modis_block below (loading
  # + clamping) can branch over them the same way composite_gpp_rast_viirs_frozen_block/
  # min_temp_raster_block already do, rather than one single ~6h target covering the whole 2000-2026
  # archive at once. gpp_files_modis itself stays one unbranched download (MODIS is frozen, fetched
  # once as a whole archive, above) -- filter_gpp_files_by_year() (r/b_filter_gpp_files_by_year.R)
  # is what turns that one flat file list into each block's own subset.
  tar_target(modis_year_blocks, build_year_blocks(2000:lubridate::year(as.Date(gpp_modis_end_date))), iteration = "list"),

  # VIIRS's own yearly calendar blocks (2012+) -- needed before any VIIRS download below can run.
  tar_target(gpp_viirs_blocks, build_year_blocks(2012:lubridate::year(as.Date(todays_date)), block_size = 1), iteration = "list"),
  tar_target(gpp_viirs_frozen_blocks, gpp_viirs_blocks[seq_len(length(gpp_viirs_blocks) - 2)], iteration = "list"),
  tar_target(gpp_viirs_recent_blocks, gpp_viirs_blocks[(length(gpp_viirs_blocks) - 1):length(gpp_viirs_blocks)], iteration = "list"),

  # Download VIIRS gap-filled (2012+), frozen (complete) blocks.
  tar_file(gpp_files_viirs_frozen_block, download_gpp_block(
    block_years    = gpp_viirs_frozen_blocks,
    roi            = covariate_download_region,
    out_dir_base   = "raw_data/predictor_variables/gpp/viirs",
    earthdata_user = "mwr25",
    product        = "VNP17A2GF.002",
    end_date_cap   = todays_date
  ), pattern = map(gpp_viirs_frozen_blocks)),

  # Same download, just the two most recent (still-catching-up) blocks.
  tar_file(gpp_files_viirs_recent_block, download_gpp_block(
    block_years    = gpp_viirs_recent_blocks,
    roi            = covariate_download_region,
    out_dir_base   = "raw_data/predictor_variables/gpp/viirs",
    earthdata_user = "mwr25",
    product        = "VNP17A2GF.002",
    end_date_cap   = todays_date
  ), pattern = map(gpp_viirs_recent_blocks)),

  # Download VIIRS non-gap-filled (near-real-time fallback).
  tar_file(gpp_files_viirs_nongf, download_gpp(
    roi            = covariate_download_region,
    out_dir        = "raw_data/predictor_variables/gpp/viirs_nongf",
    earthdata_user = "mwr25",
    product        = "VNP17A2.002",
    start_date     = paste0(gpp_viirs_recent_blocks[[1]], "-01-01"),
    end_date       = todays_date,
    job_name       = paste0("gpp_viirs_nongf_", format(Sys.Date(), "%Y%m%d")),
    time_out       = 28800)),

### ii. Load and clamp NASA composites (composite grain)

`load_and_clamp_gpp_composites()` loads each raw NASA source's own composites, clamps sensor sentinel/fill codes, and converts to a true daily rate -- deliberately NOT off-shore-masked or aggregated to monthly yet. Everything through `v.` below works at this same composite grain -- one layer per 8-day composite date, not per month -- so bias-checking/correcting NASA's own sources can match by exact date instead of a coarser "which months/years are complete enough" heuristic. Off-shore masking and period aggregation are both deferred to `vi.` below instead, run once on the finished, spliced record, rather than four times separately on each raw source before correction -- see `finish_gpp_period_raster()`'s own header (vi. below) for the full reasoning behind that split.

Two masking steps still matter here, even though only one of them (the sentinel/fill-code clamp) actually runs at this stage. Neither is real GPP, and both would corrupt a period mean if left in: the fill/sentinel codes themselves, and ocean pixels, which report small non-fill "noise" values rather than the reserved code, so the sentinel/fill-code clamp alone can't catch them -- `aus_shp` (the Australian coastline) is what catches those instead, via the off-shore mask, since several structured-survey subregions sit directly on the coast where that matters. The sentinel/fill-code clamp (`clamp_gpp_sentinel_codes()`) has to happen HERE, though, before any bias-check/correction step that averages across composites -- it can vary per composite date even at a fixed land pixel (a cloud-contaminated or sensor-glitched value on one date, at an otherwise perfectly good location), so deferring it risks a single garbage value skewing a mean-based correction ratio. The off-shore mask (`mask_gpp_offshore()`) has no such constraint -- a fixed geographic set of cells regardless of date -- so it's safe to defer all the way to `vi.` below.


```{r}
#| label: fig-gpp-masking-coastal-detail
#| fig-cap: "Example of masking steps in practice, at native ~500m resolution near the structured-survey paddock closest to the coast (~475m away, Yorke Peninsula, SA). (a) Raw composite -- ocean pegged to the sentinel fill code. (b) After the valid_max clamp -- most ocean turns NA, but a few genuinely-ocean cells (red outlines) survive with noise-level values indistinguishable from real, low-GPP land. (c) The coastline mask (white line) removes those too, plus any other cell with real (non-trivial) ocean coverage, not just the fully-ocean ones outlined in red -- by location, not value."
# no fig-asp override here -- this chunk's own coord_sf() forces a true lat/lon aspect per panel,
# and the document's own default fig-asp (0.55, see YAML front matter) happens to already give
# each of the 3 panels enough height to reach the full 8-inch figure width; the previously-tried
# 0.4 override left the panels width-starved, since a shorter figure forces smaller (still
# fixed-aspect) panels, leaving unused margin on both sides instead of using the full width
# (confirmed live by comparing rendered output at both settings).

# A concrete, fine-scale demonstration of the pipeline's two masking steps
# (this section's own text above) -- clamp_gpp_sentinel_codes() and
# mask_gpp_offshore(), now run at different pipeline stages (ii.
# and vi. respectively) -- decomposed here so the specific cells the
# coastline half catches -- that the clamp alone misses -- are visible on
# their own. paddock_id 4028663 (Yorke Peninsula, SA) is the closest
# structured-survey paddock to the coast anywhere in this pipeline's own
# paddock dataset (~475m from the coastline, confirmed live) -- chosen so
# this is a real location this pipeline's own data actually depends on, not
# an arbitrary stretch of coast.
coastal_paddock_lon <- 135.251404 # paddock_id 4028663's own centroid
coastal_paddock_lat <- -34.147325
half_deg <- 0.06 # ~6.5km half-width -- fine enough to resolve individual ~500m pixels
coastal_bbox <- terra::ext(coastal_paddock_lon - half_deg, coastal_paddock_lon + half_deg,
                            coastal_paddock_lat - half_deg, coastal_paddock_lat + half_deg)

# One real composite, picked from the pipeline's own tracked file list (not a
# hard-coded raw file path) so this stays tied to whatever this pipeline has
# actually downloaded rather than assuming one specific file exists outside
# targets' own dependency graph. Confirmed live: this exact date's own count
# of "coastline-only" cells (below) is identical across every 2013 composite
# checked, so the date itself isn't a cherry-pick -- any would show the same pattern.
gf_frozen_dates <- as.Date(sub(".*doy([0-9]{4})([0-9]{3}).*", "\\1-\\2", basename(gpp_files_viirs_frozen_block)), format = "%Y-%j")
demo_file <- gpp_files_viirs_frozen_block[which(gf_frozen_dates == as.Date("2013-06-10"))[1]]
# gpp_files_viirs_frozen_block's own paths are project-root-relative (targets'
# own convention), but quarto executes with the working directory set to this
# .qmd file's own folder -- same reason store_path/r_path exist above -- so
# this needs the identical project-root prefix before reading the file directly.
demo_file <- file.path(if (dir.exists("_targets")) "." else "..", demo_file)

raw_composite <- terra::crop(terra::rast(demo_file), coastal_bbox)
names(raw_composite) <- "value"

# Stage 2: clamp_gpp_sentinel_codes() alone -- the real ii. step, in isolation.
valid_max_only <- clamp_gpp_sentinel_codes(raw_composite, valid_max = 3)
names(valid_max_only) <- "value"

# Stage 3: both real steps together (clamp_gpp_sentinel_codes() then mask_gpp_offshore(), as vi. applies it to the finished record).
fully_masked <- mask_gpp_offshore(valid_max_only, aus_shp)
names(fully_masked) <- "value"

# The specific cells the coastline mask alone catches -- ocean (per
# aus_shp) but still non-NA after the valid_max clamp alone, i.e. exactly the
# "small non-fill noise value" cells this section's own text above describes.
ocean_only_mask <- terra::mask(raw_composite, terra::vect(aus_shp))
coastline_only_catches <- is.na(terra::values(ocean_only_mask)) & !is.na(terra::values(valid_max_only))
noise_cell_xy <- as.data.frame(terra::xyFromCell(raw_composite, which(coastline_only_catches)))

to_df <- function(r, stage) as.data.frame(r, xy = TRUE) |> dplyr::mutate(stage = stage)
masking_stages_df <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  to_df(raw_composite, "a) Raw composite"),
  to_df(valid_max_only, "b) valid_max clamp only"),
  to_df(fully_masked, "c) + aus_shp coastline mask")
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(stage = factor(stage, levels = c("a) Raw composite", "b) valid_max clamp only", "c) + aus_shp coastline mask")))

coastline_crop <- sf::st_crop(aus_shp, coastal_bbox)
pixel_res_deg <- terra::res(raw_composite)[1]

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = masking_stages_df, aes(x, y, fill = value)) +
  geom_sf(data = coastline_crop, fill = NA, colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.5, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_tile(data = dplyr::mutate(noise_cell_xy, stage = factor("b) valid_max clamp only", levels = levels(masking_stages_df$stage))),
            aes(x, y), width = pixel_res_deg, height = pixel_res_deg, fill = NA, colour = "#e41a1c", linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~stage, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "GPP (kg C/m²/8-day)", option = "C", limits = c(0, 0.03), oob = scales::squish, na.value = "grey85") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(coastal_paddock_lon - half_deg, coastal_paddock_lon + half_deg),
           ylim = c(coastal_paddock_lat - half_deg, coastal_paddock_lat + half_deg), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  # legend.position = "bottom" -- this plot's own 3 long facet titles ("a) Raw composite" etc.)
  # leave little spare width for a right-hand legend column; a first attempt forcing a tall,
  # narrow right-hand colorbar (guide_colorbar(barheight = ...)) squeezed the panels enough to
  # clip those titles and overlap the bar's own tick labels (confirmed live in the actual
  # rendered report -- not reproducible in a bare test with short placeholder facet titles, so
  # this was only caught by testing with the real title text). A horizontal bar along the full
  # figure width at the bottom has no such competition for space.
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom")
```

Like the download step (i. above), `composite_gpp_rast_viirs_frozen_block` carries its own branching one level downstream -- `pattern = map(gpp_files_viirs_frozen_block)` in the code below converts each frozen year's files to a composite-grain raster as its own independent branch, rather than one command processing every year at once. These per-year branches get combined back into two separate stacks: `composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf` (frozen + recent, the full current record) and `composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf_frozen` (frozen only).

MODIS is also branched over 5-year `modis_year_blocks` (`composite_gpp_rast_modis_block`/`modis_year_blocks`, `filter_gpp_files_by_year()`), even though `gpp_files_modis` itself is one single, unbranched download (i. above, MODIS is frozen and fetched once as a whole archive) -- without this, an unrelated pipeline-settings change, or even a single bad file anywhere in the 26-year archive (a OneDrive dataless placeholder), would force a full redo of loading and clamping every year (a rebuild that can run for hours), not just whichever one was actually affected. Branching over these blocks and recombining via `combine_spatraster_list()` (a plain concatenation here, since the blocks never overlap) isolates that cost the same way VIIRS's own frozen blocks already do, with no change to `composite_gpp_rast_modis` itself or anything downstream of it. Both this and VIIRS's own composite-loading branches (and SILO's equivalent min-temp aggregation, elsewhere in the pipeline) run on a separate, deliberately smaller "heavy" `targets`/`crew` worker pool (2 concurrent workers, vs. 4 for everything else) rather than the pipeline's default pool, since running four of these memory-heavy loads at once exhausts available RAM and crashes multiple workers mid-run -- capping concurrency just for this handful of targets avoids that without reducing parallelism anywhere else.

That split matters for caching, not just correctness. `composite_gpp_rast_viirs_recent_block` changes on essentially every `tar_make()` call as the still-open recent block keeps catching up (i. above), so anything depending on the *full* `composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf` invalidates just as often. The MOD17-vs-VNP17 bias check and pixel-scale correction (iii./iv.) use the *frozen-only* stack instead, since using the full stack there would rerun that pair of steps (\~1h combined) from scratch on every single run with new VIIRS data, undoing the exact stability this pipeline's own frozen/recent split is built to provide. The GF-vs-NGF bias check and correction can't be stabilised the same way, though -- `composite_gpp_rast_viirs_nongf` only ever covers the last \~2 years by construction, so it has zero overlap with a frozen-only GF reference; those two still use, and still rerun with, the full stack. The real splice (v.) also uses the full `composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf` -- that step needs today's most complete data, not a stable reference.

#### Code

```{r}
#| label: src-targets-step-ii
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "_targets.R -- ii. Load and clamp NASA composites (composite grain)"

  # ii. Load and clamp NASA composites (composite grain) -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # load_and_clamp_gpp_composites() loads each raw source's own composites, clamps sensor sentinel/fill codes, and converts to a true daily rate -- deliberately NOT off-shore-masked or aggregated to monthly yet (see that function's own header for why those two specifically are safe to defer to vi. below, once, rather than doing them four times here). Everything below (iii.-v.) works at this same composite grain -- one layer per 8-day composite date, not per month -- so bias-checking/correcting NASA's own sources can match by exact date instead of a coarser "which months/years are complete enough" heuristic.

  # MODIS: the full 2000 to gpp_modis_end_date archive (i. above), not just 2000-2011 -- only ever ends up in the merged record (v. below) where VIIRS genuinely has no data (2012+ VIIRS is used automatically, see combine_spatraster_list()'s own header).
  # Branched over modis_year_blocks, one calendar block per branch -- same reasoning as composite_gpp_rast_viirs_frozen_block/min_temp_raster_block below: without this, a single ~6h monolithic target here would mean an unrelated pipeline-settings change, or one bad file anywhere in the archive (a single OneDrive dataless placeholder), forces a full ~6h redo of all 26 years, not just the one block actually affected. Recombined into the same composite_gpp_rast_modis name every downstream target already expects (gpp_modis_bias_check/gpp_modis_pixel_ratio_rast/composite_gpp_rast_modis_corrected/gpp_modis_national_mean/gpp_modis_paddock_mean below all keep working unchanged) via combine_spatraster_list() -- same recombination function VIIRS's own frozen blocks already use, non-overlapping blocks by construction so this is a plain concatenation in practice, not genuine merge-precedence logic.
  tar_terra_rast(
    composite_gpp_rast_modis_block,
    load_and_clamp_gpp_composites(filter_gpp_files_by_year(gpp_files_modis, modis_year_blocks)),
    pattern   = map(modis_year_blocks),
    gdal      = covariate_gdal_options,
    resources = heavy_resources
  ),
  tar_terra_rast(composite_gpp_rast_modis, combine_spatraster_list(composite_gpp_rast_modis_block), gdal = covariate_gdal_options),

  # VIIRS gap-filled, frozen (complete, no longer changing) blocks -- one branch per calendar-year block.
  tar_terra_rast(
    composite_gpp_rast_viirs_frozen_block,
    load_and_clamp_gpp_composites(gpp_files_viirs_frozen_block),
    pattern   = map(gpp_files_viirs_frozen_block),
    gdal      = covariate_gdal_options,
    resources = heavy_resources
  ),

  # VIIRS gap-filled, recent (still-catching-up) blocks -- plain gap-filled only, no non-gap-filled fallback spliced in here; that happens later, at the merge in v., not per-composite-date -- see combine_spatraster_list()'s own header for why that's safe.
  tar_terra_rast(
    composite_gpp_rast_viirs_recent_block,
    load_and_clamp_gpp_composites(gpp_files_viirs_recent_block),
    gdal      = covariate_gdal_options,
    resources = heavy_resources
  ),

  # VIIRS gap-filled, frozen + recent combined -- the full, current, clean gap-filled record, used by the real splice (v.), and by the GF-vs-NGF bias check/correction (iii./iv.) -- those two specifically NEED the recent block, since composite_gpp_rast_viirs_nongf only ever covers the recent ~2 years by construction and so has zero overlap with frozen-only GF (see gpp_gf_bias_check's own comment, iii. below). Not used by the MOD17-vs-VNP17 bias check/correction, though -- that pair is stabilised on the frozen-only stack instead (composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf_frozen, below), which GF-vs-NGF can't use given the zero-overlap constraint above.
  tar_terra_rast(composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf, combine_spatraster_list(c(composite_gpp_rast_viirs_frozen_block, list(composite_gpp_rast_viirs_recent_block))), gdal = covariate_gdal_options),

  # VIIRS gap-filled, FROZEN ONLY -- a stable reference that only changes once a year (when a block gets promoted out of "recent"), unlike composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf above, which changes on essentially every tar_make() call as the still-open recent block keeps catching up. Used by the MOD17-vs-VNP17 bias check and pixel-scale correction (iii./iv.) instead of the full GF stack, so that pair of steps (~1h combined) doesn't rerun on every recent-block catch-up. Not usable for the GF-vs-NGF bias check/correction, though (see composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf's own comment above and gpp_gf_bias_check's, iii. below) -- that pair still reruns on every recent-block catch-up, an accepted, structural cost of NGF's own recency-limited download window (i. above), not something this target can fix.
  tar_terra_rast(composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf_frozen, combine_spatraster_list(composite_gpp_rast_viirs_frozen_block), gdal = covariate_gdal_options),

  # VIIRS non-gap-filled -- the full accumulated record (download_gpp() never deletes old files, so this already reaches back further than the 2-year window gpp_files_viirs_nongf itself requests, i. above).
  tar_terra_rast(
    composite_gpp_rast_viirs_nongf,
    load_and_clamp_gpp_composites(gpp_files_viirs_nongf),
    gdal      = covariate_gdal_options,
    resources = heavy_resources
  ),

### iii. Cross-product bias-check diagnostics {#sec-gpp-bias-check}

NASA products only -- PML's own diagnostic lives in ix. below instead, alongside its own correction, once both finished products (this section's `monthly_gpp_rast`, B)'s `pml_gpp_rast`) exist. This pipeline splices together two pairs of NASA sources built at the same underlying spec but different processing levels or instruments -- VIIRS gap-filled against its own non-gap-filled near-real-time fallback (same sensor, different processing level); MOD17 against VNP17 directly, over their own real 2012+ overlap (downloading MOD17's full archive rather than stopping at 2011, i. above, is what makes this comparison possible at all). Even sources this closely related can disagree systematically in level, so it's important to check for that bias directly, before deciding whether, and how, to correct it.

Process: compare the two products wherever they both actually cover, at both correlation (do they broadly move together?) and bias (is there a level offset even when they do?). A real, persistent offset despite strong correlation is the pattern [iv. Compute NASA pixel-scale corrections](#sec-gpp-pixel-corrections) below is designed to fix.

**Here, specifically:** one shared function, `compare_gpp_rasters()`, applies this twice, both at composite grain (ii. above) rather than monthly -- gap-filled against non-gap-filled VIIRS, over their full accumulated overlap; MOD17 against VNP17, over their real 2012+ overlap. Only the MOD17-vs-VNP17 one uses the *frozen-only* gap-filled VIIRS stack (`composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf_frozen`, ii. above), a caching stability choice; the GF-vs-NGF comparison can't be stabilised the same way, since non-gap-filled VIIRS only ever covers the recent \~2 years by construction and so has zero overlap with a frozen-only reference (ii. above). Every raster here already shares the same 500m grid and gC/m²/day units (ii. above), so no resampling is needed within this NASA-only section -- that's only ever needed against PML's own coarser grid, ix. below. `compare_gpp_rasters()` itself has no product-specific knowledge at all -- it just matches by whatever layer name (here, a plain composite date) both sides share, extracts at paddock locations and compares.

Both compare at paddock locations specifically, not raster-wide -- a whole-raster version of this check (comparing all \~32M pixels across the full east extent) finds a tiny median difference but a surprisingly low correlation (\~0.15), diluted by the vast non-agricultural majority of the raster (ocean, desert, urban) where both products report near-zero, mostly-noise GPP with no real signal to correlate. Both results feed directly into the ratio corrections computed in [iv. Compute NASA pixel-scale corrections](#sec-gpp-pixel-corrections) below, including MOD17 vs VNP17. A **paddock** here is this project's own spatial survey unit.

Both diagnostics' own results (@fig-agreement-by-month, in [Correction and Splice Diagnostics](#sec-gpp-figures) at the end of this document -- rows a/b, PML's own third comparison there is introduced separately in ix. below) show a real, systematic level offset despite generally strong correlation (the two sides broadly agree on *when* GPP rises and falls, just not always on its exact *level*) -- precisely the pattern the ratio correction (iv. below) is designed to fix. A plain chronological time series buries any seasonal shape in year-to-year noise, so both are shown by calendar month instead -- the one grouping that actually matters here, since [iv. Compute NASA pixel-scale corrections](#sec-gpp-pixel-corrections)'s own ratio correction is computed independently *per calendar month*, not just per pixel.

#### Code

```{r}

#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "_targets.R -- iii. Cross-product bias-check diagnostics"

  # iii. Determine bias in NASA products   ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # each call site pre-aligning its own two rasters onto a common grid/grain/units first; every raster here already shares the same 500m grid and gC/m^2/day units (ii. above), so no resampling is needed within this NASA-only section

  # Diagnostic: how well gap-filled and non-gap-filled VIIRS agree, over their full overlap -- MUST use the full (frozen+recent) GF stack here, not composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf_frozen: composite_gpp_rast_viirs_nongf only ever covers the last ~2 years by construction (download_gpp()'s own recent-block-matching window, i. above), so it has ZERO overlap with frozen-only GF (confirmed live: build_gpp_pixel_ratio_raster() errors "share no layers in common" if this is tried) -- unlike the MODIS correction below, whose own reference (composite_gpp_rast_modis) genuinely spans frozen years too, this one structurally needs the recent block to have any data to compare against at all, so it can't be stabilised the same way. intersect() inside compare_gpp_rasters() finds the real overlap on its own, matching by exact composite date. rast_a = non-gap-filled, rast_b = gap-filled -- positive bias_mean means gap-filled reads higher.
  gpp_gf_bias_check = compare_gpp_rasters(composite_gpp_rast_viirs_nongf, composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf, structured_survey_points),

  # Diagnostic: how well MOD17 and VNP17 agree, over the frozen portion of their real 2012+ overlap -- composite_gpp_rast_modis is the untrimmed full archive (i. above), composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf_frozen is pure, stable VIIRS (ii. above), so intersect() inside compare_gpp_rasters() finds the overlap on its own, again by exact composite date. rast_a = MODIS, rast_b = VIIRS -- positive bias_mean means VIIRS reads higher.
  gpp_modis_bias_check = compare_gpp_rasters(composite_gpp_rast_modis, composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf_frozen, structured_survey_points),

### iv. Compute NASA pixel-scale corrections {#sec-gpp-pixel-corrections}

This is a general-purpose ratio-correction method which applies to wherever two remote-sensing products need to be joined into one series, regardless of region or the quantity being spliced (GPP or otherwise).

The function computes, independently at every pixel (500 m, both NASA sources share this native resolution) and every calendar month, the ratio `mean(numerator) / mean(denominator)` averaged across every composite date both sides cover.

This also mirrors PML-V2's own published approach to a structurally identical problem: PML-V2 itself is spliced from two different satellite eras internally (older AVHRR inputs pre-2000, then MODIS/VIIRS-family inputs after), and its developers' own analysis: Xu et al. (2026) explicitly considered and rejected a "unidirectional" (i.e. single, uniformly-applied) scaling correction for that internal splice, adopting instead what they call a "pixel-scale bidirectional consolidation" -- correcting at the resolution of individual pixels rather than any single global/regional factor.

The pixel / month specific offset is important due to structural biases in satellite data. This is because:

(1) GPP is a physically non-negative quantity, and MOD17/VNP17's own bias is consistent enough not to be safely subtracted uniformly without risking a negative result -- a *ratio* correction rescales the signal proportionally instead, and (being a multiplication by a positive number) can never turn a non-negative value negative the way a flat subtraction can. This mirrors a standard convention in satellite/climate bias correction more broadly: a multiplicative (ratio) correction is generally preferred over an additive one specifically for quantities bounded at zero (GPP, precipitation, evapotranspiration), for exactly this reason.
(2) A raw source's value at structured-survey paddocks can differ from its own national mean (paddocks sit in productive grain-growing regions) -- so a single factor calibrated at a handful of paddocks and applied nationally doesn't generalise spatially -- [x. National + paddock mean diagnostics](#sec-gpp-national-paddock) below has the actual national-vs-paddock numbers. A pixel-scale ratio solves both at once.

I use the same function, `build_gpp_pixel_ratio_raster()`, to compute both of A)'s own splice corrections (PML's own correction, C) below, uses it a third time):

- MODIS splice: corrects MOD17 *towards* the pipeline's own gap-filled VIIRS record, from their real 2012+ composite-date overlap.
- VIIRS near-real-time splice: corrects non-gap-filled VIIRS *towards* gap-filled VIIRS, from their accumulated composite-date overlap.

Only the MODIS one uses the *frozen-only* gap-filled VIIRS stack as its reference (`composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf_frozen`, ii. above); the VIIRS one still uses, and still reruns with, the full stack, since non-gap-filled VIIRS only ever covers the recent \~2 years by construction and so has zero overlap with a frozen-only reference (ii. above). Both corrected outputs are still applied to each source's own *full* range regardless (`composite_gpp_rast_modis`/`composite_gpp_rast_viirs_nongf` in full, not restricted to frozen years) -- only the MODIS ratio itself is fitted from a stable reference.

Both corrections run at composite grain (ii. above), not monthly -- `months_of` (a plan-time helper, `_targets.R`) tells `build_gpp_pixel_ratio_raster()`/`apply_gpp_pixel_ratio_correction()` how to read a calendar month out of a date-named layer instead of their own default `"<month>_<year>"` convention (see each function's own header). `apply_gpp_pixel_ratio_correction()` then applies each fitted ratio to its own raw source's full range. See @fig-pixel-ratio-maps and @fig-splice-continuity, in [Correction and Splice Diagnostics](#sec-gpp-figures) at the end of this document, for these corrections in practice.

#### Code

```{r}
#| label: src-targets-step-iv
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "_targets.R -- iv. Compute NASA pixel-scale corrections"

  # iv. Compute NASA pixel-scale corrections -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # MOD17 towards VNP17, and non-gap-filled towards gap-filled VIIRS -- both NASA-internal, both at composite grain still (months_of below tells build_gpp_pixel_ratio_raster()/apply_gpp_pixel_ratio_correction() how to read a calendar month out of a date-named layer instead of their own default month_year-named convention -- see each function's own header). PML's own correction lives in ix. below instead, once this section's own finished monthly_gpp_rast (vi. below) exists as its reference.
  composite_gpp_months_of <- function(x) lubridate::month(as.Date(x)),

  # Pixel-scale ratio correction for MODIS -- towards VIIRS's own level, from their real 2012+ overlap, restricted to the FROZEN (stable) portion of VIIRS (composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf_frozen vs composite_gpp_rast_modis, ii./i. above) -- frozen so this correction doesn't refit every time the still-open recent block picks up a new composite; intersect() inside build_gpp_pixel_ratio_raster() finds the overlap on its own.
  tar_terra_rast(gpp_modis_pixel_ratio_rast, build_gpp_pixel_ratio_raster(composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf_frozen, composite_gpp_rast_modis, months_of = composite_gpp_months_of), gdal = covariate_gdal_options),

  # Corrected MODIS, full range -- only its pre-2012 portion ever ends up in the merged record below (VIIRS is used automatically for 2012+, where both cover a period), so no separate pre-2012 trim is needed -- see combine_spatraster_list()'s own header for why.
  tar_terra_rast(composite_gpp_rast_modis_corrected, apply_gpp_pixel_ratio_correction(composite_gpp_rast_modis, gpp_modis_pixel_ratio_rast, months_of = composite_gpp_months_of), gdal = covariate_gdal_options),

  # Pixel-scale ratio correction for VIIRS -- from the full GF vs full NGF record (ii. above); MUST use the full (frozen+recent) GF stack here, not composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf_frozen -- see gpp_gf_bias_check's own comment above for why (composite_gpp_rast_viirs_nongf only covers the recent ~2 years by construction, so it has zero overlap with frozen-only GF). intersect() inside build_gpp_pixel_ratio_raster() finds their real overlap on its own; no "correction years" pre-filter needed.
  tar_terra_rast(gpp_gf_pixel_ratio_rast, build_gpp_pixel_ratio_raster(composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf, composite_gpp_rast_viirs_nongf, months_of = composite_gpp_months_of), gdal = covariate_gdal_options),

  # Corrected non-gap-filled VIIRS, full range -- only its dates where gap-filled hasn't published yet ever end up in the merged record below (GF is used automatically, where both cover a period), so no separate per-composite-date splice function is needed -- see combine_spatraster_list()'s own header for why.
  tar_terra_rast(composite_gpp_rast_viirs_nongf_corrected, apply_gpp_pixel_ratio_correction(composite_gpp_rast_viirs_nongf, gpp_gf_pixel_ratio_rast, months_of = composite_gpp_months_of), gdal = covariate_gdal_options),

```

### v. Splice NASA sources into one continuous stack {#sec-gpp-splice}

Still at composite grain -- `combine_spatraster_list()` merges every corrected NASA source into one continuous stack, most-robust-source-first: gap-filled VIIRS (frozen + recent, wherever it actually has real data, ii. above), then corrected non-gap-filled VIIRS as the fallback for whatever gap-filled hasn't published yet, then corrected MOD17 as the final fallback for anything VIIRS doesn't cover at all (iv. above) -- not a plain concatenation (see that function's own header for why this matters now that MOD17 is downloaded in full rather than pre-trimmed to a non-overlapping window). Both NASA-internal corrections run at composite grain and produce a full corrected range each, so `combine_spatraster_list()`'s own priority ordering handles every fallback case on its own, with no product-specific splice logic needed anywhere in this step.

All three splices in this record get a real pixel-scale correction -- MOD17 into VIIRS and non-gap-filled into gap-filled VIIRS from iv. above, PML into the finished NASA record from ix. below. Correcting the MOD17-into-VIIRS boundary needs a real overlapping window to compute a ratio from, which is why MOD17's full available archive is downloaded (i. above) rather than stopping at 2011: it gives a real, overlapping 2012+ stretch to compare MOD17 against VNP17 with directly (iii. above), rather than leaning on the two products' shared specification alone. See @fig-gpp-splice-timeline above (Overview), which marks every boundary and shows which raw product supplies each stretch of the finished record.

#### Code

```{r}

#| eval: false
#| echo: true

  # v. Splice NASA sources into one continuous stack ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Still composite grain -- merge every source into one continuous stack, most-robust-source-first: gap-filled VIIRS (frozen + recent, wherever it actually has real data), then corrected non-gap-filled VIIRS as the fallback for whatever gap-filled hasn't published yet, then corrected MODIS as the final fallback for anything VIIRS doesn't cover at all (not raw MODIS -- iv. above).
  tar_terra_rast(composite_gpp_rast, combine_spatraster_list(list(composite_gpp_rast_viirs_gf, composite_gpp_rast_viirs_nongf_corrected, composite_gpp_rast_modis_corrected)), gdal = covariate_gdal_options),

This produces `monthly_gpp_rast`: NASA's finished, self-contained monthly product -- everything from i. through here (A) never touches PML at all, matching this section's own opening description of the three-part A)/B)/C) design.

## B) PML {#sec-gpp-pml}

PML-V2's own download and crop steps are fully self-contained -- no dependency on anything A) NASA built, and vice versa (A) never touches PML). 

### vii. Download PML

A fixed, closed historical archive (1982-2020) with no dependency on the current date -- once downloaded via `download_pml_data()`, `tar_make()` never re-triggers it again (barring a code or region change).

### viii. Crop PML to same area

PML-V2 is a global product so is cropped to the region of interest `covariate_download_region` (+ 0.5 degree margin) so downstream processing functions are computationally efficient, then masked to that same region's polygon and to `aus_shp`'s coastline (`mask_gpp_offshore()`, the same masking step A) NASA's own record uses in vi.) so both finished products share the same real-world footprint. This occurs right after `build_pml_gpp_raster()` converts its raw monthly-total NetCDFs to the same mean-daily-rate convention (gC/m²/day) the rest of the pipeline uses (see that function's own unit-conversion note below). PML-V2 needs no period aggregation of its own (it's already monthly) -- this is all of B).

#### Code

```{r}
#| label: src-targets-step-viii
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "_targets.R -- viii. Crop PML to same area"

  # viii. Crop PML to same area ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # PML-V2 is a global product (1500x3600 cells), ~85x more than this pipeline ever needs -- cropping right after download keeps every downstream target's storage/IO footprint small. Split into two steps, not one: pml_gpp_rast_cropped (crop only, real PML values) is this pipeline's own actual standard grid -- also the sole ingredient of covariate_grid_template (section 1), the geometry-only target every resample_to_grid() TEMPLATE use (rainfall/soil_moisture/min_temp, and this section's own monthly_gpp_rast_coarse, ix. below) depends on instead of on pml_gpp_rast directly, since that function only ever reads a template's geometry, never its values (see its own header). pml_gpp_rast itself then masks pml_gpp_rast_cropped further (real DATA, not geometry) to covariate_download_region's own polygon and aus_shp's coastline, matching NASA's own finished record footprint (covariate_download_region's own polygon at download, aus_shp via mask_gpp_offshore() in vi.) -- without this, raw PML's own bbox+margin crop alone would leave real values across ~16,000 more nationally-averaged cells than NASA's own masked record has, corrupting any raw-PML-vs-pipeline-output national-mean comparison. Both aus_shp and covariate_download_region are shared, section-agnostic inputs (not NASA's own output), so masking to them here doesn't break A)/B)'s own independence. See build_gpp_pixel_ratio_raster()'s own header for how this also shrinks (though doesn't eliminate) the NA-vs-ratio=1 edge case its own pixel-scale correction was built to handle. The pml_gpp_rast_cropped/pml_gpp_rast split itself exists because a single combined target would mean ANY future PML-only change -- this masking step included -- invalidates every one of those geometry-only downstream consumers too, cascading all the way through the plague HMM and its own reports/shiny deployment for a change that never touched the grid at all (~104 targets, confirmed live).
  tar_terra_rast(pml_gpp_rast_cropped, {
    r <- build_pml_gpp_raster(pml_gpp_files)
    bbox <- sf::st_bbox(covariate_download_region)
    margin_deg <- 0.5
    terra::crop(r, terra::ext(bbox["xmin"] - margin_deg, bbox["xmax"] + margin_deg, bbox["ymin"] - margin_deg, bbox["ymax"] + margin_deg))
  }, gdal = covariate_gdal_options),

  tar_terra_rast(pml_gpp_rast, {
    r <- terra::mask(pml_gpp_rast_cropped, terra::vect(covariate_download_region))
    mask_gpp_offshore(r, aus_shp)
  }, gdal = covariate_gdal_options),

  ## C) Combine =================================================================================================================================================
